questions.question: A sparse matrix is a matrix in which:

options.B: The number of rows equals the number of columns
options.D: Most of the elements are zero

questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: Storing only the non-zero elements saves memory.

questions.question: A 100 × 100 sparse matrix has 50 non-zero elements. In the triplet (row, column, value) form with one header row, how many values are stored?
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: (50 + 1) rows × 3 columns = 153, instead of 10,000.

questions.question: The 'fast transpose' algorithm for a sparse matrix in triplet form runs in time proportional to:
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: It first counts the terms in each column and computes their starting positions.

questions.question: A lower triangular n × n matrix has how many elements on or below the main diagonal?
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: For n = 10 this is 55.

questions.question: A 10 × 10 lower triangular matrix is stored row by row, keeping only elements on or below the diagonal (1-based indices). How many elements come before A[5][3]?

questions.explanation: Rows 1–4 contribute 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, plus 2 elements before A[5][3] in row 5.

questions.question: A tridiagonal n × n matrix has at most how many non-zero elements?
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: The main diagonal (n) plus the diagonals above and below it (n − 1 each); for n = 10, 28.

questions.question: The polynomial 3x⁵ + 2x² + 7 is stored in an array indexed by exponent. The array needs at least:
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices

questions.question: A dynamic array that doubles its capacity when it is full gives an append operation that costs:
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: Occasional O(n) copies are spread over many cheap appends.

I. Row-major order stores all elements of a row together.

Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The triplet representation saves space only when the matrix is sparse.
II. Matrix addition in triplet form can be done by merging the two triplet lists.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Arrays and Sparse Matrices
questions.explanation: Merging by (row, column) order adds matching terms.

questions.question:

options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Storing a sparse matrix in triplet form saves memory.
Reason (R): The triplet form stores every zero element as well.

options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Binary search needs a sorted array.

options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question: A stack follows the principle:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Insertion (push) and deletion (pop) happen at the same end, the top.

questions.question: Starting with an empty stack, the operations push 1, push 2, push 3, pop, push 4, pop, pop remove the elements in the order:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: After popping 3, 4 is pushed on top of 2, so 4 and then 2 come out.

questions.question: Elements 1, 2, 3, 4 are pushed in this order, with pops allowed at any time. Which output sequence is IMPOSSIBLE?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Popping 4 first leaves 3 on top, so 1 cannot come next.

questions.question: How many different output sequences can be produced by passing 1, 2, 3 through a stack?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: The count is the Catalan number C₃ = 5; only 3, 1, 2 is impossible.

questions.question: With n = 4 elements pushed in order through a stack, the number of possible output permutations is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Catalan number C₄ = 14.

questions.question: The postfix form of  A + B * C − D  is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: B * C is formed first, then added to A, then D is subtracted.

questions.question: The postfix form of  (A + B) * (C − D)  is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: The prefix form would be * + A B − C D.

questions.question: The value of the postfix expression  6 2 3 + − 3 8 2 / + *  is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications

questions.question: The value of the prefix expression  − * 2 3 4  is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications

questions.question: The prefix form of  A * B + C  is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: The last operator applied, +, comes first.

questions.question: While evaluating the postfix expression  2 3 4 * +  with a stack, the maximum number of elements on the stack at one time is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: 2, 3 and 4 are all on the stack before * is applied.

questions.question: Which string of brackets is balanced?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket – checked with a stack.

questions.question: In an array implementation of a stack of size MAX (0-based), with top = −1 meaning empty, the stack is full when:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Pushing when full causes overflow; popping when empty causes underflow.

questions.question: Two stacks share one array of size n by growing from opposite ends. Overflow occurs only when:

options.A: The total number of elements in both stacks reaches n
options.D: Both stacks hold the same number of elements

questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: This uses the space more flexibly than a fixed half each.

questions.question: Pushing onto a stack implemented as a singly linked list, with the top at the head, takes:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: The new node simply becomes the new head.

questions.question: The Tower of Hanoi with 5 discs needs a minimum of how many moves?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: 2ⁿ − 1 = 31; the recursive solution uses the call stack.

questions.question: Which of the following does NOT typically use a stack?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue; depth-first search uses a stack.

questions.question:

a. Function-call management
b. Printer job scheduling
c. Depth-first search
d. Browser Back button history

1. Stack (explicit or recursion)
2. Call stack
3. Queue

questions.explanation: LIFO suits anything that must be undone in reverse order.

questions.question: During infix-to-postfix conversion, an operator on the stack is popped to the output when the incoming operator has:

options.D: Lower or equal precedence (for left-associative operators)

questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Right-associative ^ is handled differently.

questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Similarly, a queue can be built from two stacks.

questions.question: What does the stack contain (bottom → top) after: push 5, push 7, pop, push 2, push 9, pop?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: 7 and 9 are removed.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Recursion is implemented with a stack of activation records.
II. Every recursive program can be converted into an iterative one using an explicit stack.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Both are standard results.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Popping from an empty stack causes underflow.
II. Pushing onto an empty stack causes overflow.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Overflow happens when pushing onto a full stack.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: That LIFO property matches the stack exactly.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Postfix expressions need parentheses to show the order of operations.
Reason (R): In postfix notation the order of operators alone fixes the order of evaluation.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question:

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Depth-first search can be implemented with a stack.
Reason (R): A stack can be implemented with a linked list.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications
questions.explanation: Both true, but the implementation detail does not explain why DFS uses a stack.

questions.question: The infix form of the postfix expression  a b c * + d −  is:
questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications

questions.subject: Stacks and Their Applications

questions.question: The peek (top) operation on a stack:

options.C: Returns the top element without removing it

questions.question: A queue follows the principle:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Elements are added at the rear and removed from the front.

questions.question: Enqueue 1, enqueue 2, enqueue 3, dequeue, enqueue 4, dequeue. Which element is now at the front?
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: 1 and 2 have been removed; 3 then 4 remain.

questions.question: The main drawback of a simple (linear) array queue is that:

options.D: Space freed at the front cannot be reused once rear reaches the end

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: A circular queue wraps the indices around to reuse the space.

questions.question: In a circular queue of size n that keeps one slot empty, the queue is full when:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: So such a queue can hold at most n − 1 elements; rear == front means empty.

questions.question: A circular queue has 5 slots (indices 0–4). front points to the first element and rear points to the slot after the last element. If front = 3 and rear = 1, how many elements are in the queue?
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: (rear − front + n) % n = (1 − 3 + 5) % 5 = 3 (slots 3, 4 and 0).

questions.question: A double-ended queue (deque) allows:

options.A: Insertion and deletion at both ends

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: An input-restricted deque allows insertion at one end only; an output-restricted deque allows deletion at one end only.

questions.question: In a priority queue, the element removed first is:

options.B: The one with the highest priority

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Equal priorities are often served in arrival order.

questions.question: With a binary heap, the priority-queue operations insert and delete-max take:

options.D: O(log n) each, while find-max takes O(1)

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: The heap's height is ⌊log₂ n⌋.

questions.question: A priority queue kept as an UNSORTED array has insert and delete-max costs of:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: A sorted array reverses this: O(n) insert and O(1) delete.

questions.question: In an array-based binary heap with 0-based indices, the children of the node at index i are at:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: The parent of i is at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋.

questions.question: 45 is inserted into the max-heap stored as [50, 30, 40, 10, 20]. The resulting array is:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: 45 is placed at index 5; its parent (index 2) is 40, so they swap; its new parent 50 is larger, so it stops.

questions.question: The maximum is deleted from the max-heap [50, 30, 45, 10, 20, 40]. The resulting array is:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: The last element 40 moves to the root and sifts down past its larger child 45.

questions.question: Building a binary heap from n unsorted elements with the bottom-up (heapify) method takes:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Most nodes are near the bottom and need little work.

questions.question: Round-robin CPU scheduling is naturally implemented with a:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Each process gets a time slice and then goes to the back of the queue.

questions.question: Which algorithm uses a priority queue?
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Huffman coding and Prim's algorithm also use priority queues.

questions.question: Breadth-first search of a graph uses a:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Vertices are visited level by level.

questions.question: A queue implemented as a linked list with front and rear pointers supports enqueue and dequeue in:

options.A: O(1) enqueue and O(n) dequeue always

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: New nodes are added after rear; nodes are removed at front.

questions.question: A queue can be implemented with two stacks so that each operation takes:
questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues
questions.explanation: Elements are moved from the input stack to the output stack only when the output stack is empty.

questions.question: A circular queue has 8 slots, front = 6 and rear = 2 (rear points after the last element). How many free slots remain if one slot is always kept empty?

questions.question:

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues

questions.subject: Queues and Priority Queues

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

questions.explanation: Addition walks both lists in exponent order.

questions.question: Given a pointer to the LAST node of a circular singly linked list, deleting the first node takes:
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: The first node is last->next, so it can be unlinked directly.

questions.question: A structure such as  struct node { int data; struct node *next; };  is called:
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: It contains a pointer to its own type.

questions.question:
Match the list operation with its cost (singly linked list, head pointer only, n nodes):
a. Insert at the head
b. Search for a value
c. Delete the last node
d. Read the head's data

1. O(1) – a new node becomes the head
2. O(1)
3. O(n)
4. O(n) – the predecessor must be found
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Only operations near the head are constant time.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Binary search is efficient on a singly linked list.
II. Linked lists allocate memory dynamically as nodes are added.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Binary search needs random access, which linked lists lack.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In a doubly linked list, a node can be deleted in O(1) if a pointer to it is given.
II. A circular list can be traversed starting from any node.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Inserting at the head of a linked list takes O(1) time.
Reason (R): Only the new node's next pointer and the head pointer change.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: No other node is touched.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Linked lists allow random access to any element in O(1).
Reason (R): Nodes of a linked list are reached by following pointers from the head.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Following pointers makes access O(n); R shows why A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Doubly linked lists use more memory per node than singly linked lists.
Reason (R): Doubly linked lists cannot be traversed backwards.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: A is true (an extra prev pointer); R is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Circular linked lists are useful for round-robin scheduling.
Reason (R): A singly linked list node contains data and a next pointer.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Both true, but R does not explain A; the circular link does.

questions.question: The number of NULL pointers in a doubly linked list of n ≥ 1 nodes (not circular) is:
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: The first node's prev and the last node's next.

questions.question: To delete the node after node p in a singly linked list, one writes:
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: The node is unlinked before it is freed.

questions.question: An orthogonal (cross) linked list is commonly used to represent:

options.A: A sparse matrix, linking the non-zero elements by row and by column

questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Each node belongs to one row list and one column list.

questions.question: The time to concatenate two circular singly linked lists, given pointers to their last nodes, is:
questions.subject: Linked Lists
questions.explanation: Only a few pointers need to be exchanged.

questions.question: A tree with n nodes has exactly how many edges?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Every node except the root has exactly one edge to its parent.

questions.question: The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height 4 is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees

questions.question: The maximum number of nodes at level 5 of a binary tree (root at level 0) is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Level i can hold at most 2^i nodes.

questions.question: The minimum possible height of a binary tree with 100 nodes is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: ⌈log₂(101)⌉ − 1 = 7 − 1 = 6; a tree of height 5 holds at most 63 nodes.

questions.question: A binary tree has 10 nodes with two children each. How many leaves does it have?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: In any binary tree, n₀ = n₂ + 1.

questions.question: A full (strict) binary tree has 15 internal nodes. How many nodes does it have in total?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Leaves = internal + 1 = 16; total = 15 + 16 = 31 (2n + 1).

questions.question: In a complete binary tree stored in an array with 1-based indexing, the parent of the node at index 13 is at index:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Parent = ⌊i/2⌋; children of i are 2i and 2i + 1.

questions.question: A binary tree has root A; A's left child is B with children D (left) and E (right); A's right child is C with only a right child F. Its preorder traversal is:

options.A: D B E A C F
options.B: A B D E C F
options.C: D E B F C A
options.D: A B C D E F

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Preorder visits root, then left subtree, then right subtree.

questions.question: For the same tree (A; B with D, E; C with right child F), the inorder traversal is:

options.A: D B E A F C
options.B: D E B F C A
options.C: A B D E C F
options.D: D B E A C F

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Inorder: left subtree, root, right subtree.

questions.question: For the same tree (A; B with D, E; C with right child F), the postorder traversal is:

options.A: D B E F C A
options.B: A B D E C F
options.C: D E B F C A
options.D: F C E D B A

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Postorder: left subtree, right subtree, root.

questions.question: A binary tree has preorder 1 2 4 5 3 6 7 and inorder 4 2 5 1 6 3 7. Its postorder traversal is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Root 1; left subtree {4, 2, 5} with root 2; right subtree {6, 3, 7} with root 3.

questions.question: Which pair of traversals does NOT, in general, uniquely determine a binary tree?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Without inorder, a single child cannot be placed as left or right.

questions.question: How many structurally different binary trees can be formed with 3 nodes?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Catalan number C₃ = 5 (C₄ = 14).

questions.question: In the linked representation of a binary tree with n nodes, how many child pointers are NULL?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: 2n pointers in all; n − 1 of them point to children.

questions.question: A general tree or forest is usually converted into a binary tree using the:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: The first child becomes the left child and the next sibling the right child.

questions.question: A level-order (breadth-first) traversal of a binary tree is implemented with a:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Nodes are processed level by level, left to right.

questions.question: The extra space used by a recursive inorder traversal of a binary tree of height h is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: O(log n) for a balanced tree and O(n) for a skewed one.

questions.question: In the expression tree for (a + b) * c, the postorder traversal gives:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Postorder of an expression tree yields postfix notation; preorder yields prefix.

questions.question: A skewed binary tree with n nodes has height:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Every node has only one child, forming a chain.

questions.question: The height of a complete binary tree with n nodes is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: A complete tree fills every level except possibly the last.

questions.question: In a binary tree, the degree of a node is:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: In a binary tree it is 0, 1 or 2.

questions.question:
Match the traversal with its order:
a. Preorder
b. Inorder
c. Postorder
d. Level order

1. Level by level, left to right
2. Left, right, root
3. Root, left, right
4. Left, root, right
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: The names describe when the root is visited.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Every full (strict) binary tree has an odd number of nodes.
II. Every complete binary tree is a full binary tree.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: n = 2i + 1 is odd; a complete tree may have a node with one (left) child, so it need not be full.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
II. Adding one edge to a tree always creates exactly one cycle.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Both are standard properties of trees.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In any binary tree, the number of leaves is one more than the number of nodes with two children.
Reason (R): Counting edges gives n − 1 = n₁ + 2n₂, and n = n₀ + n₁ + n₂.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Substituting gives n₀ = n₂ + 1.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Preorder and postorder together always determine a unique binary tree.
Reason (R): Inorder traversal shows which nodes lie in the left and right subtrees of each root.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: R is true, and that information is missing without inorder, so A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Level-order traversal needs a queue.
Reason (R): Inorder traversal of an expression tree gives prefix notation.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – inorder gives infix notation (preorder gives prefix).

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A binary tree with n nodes can be stored in an array of size n if it is complete.
Reason (R): Complete binary trees leave no gaps in level order.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: With no gaps, index formulas locate every child and parent.

questions.question: The number of edges on the path from the root to a node is called the node's:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: Height is measured downwards to the deepest leaf.

questions.question: Storing a skewed binary tree of height 9 in an array (1-based level-order positions) may need an array of size:
questions.subject: Trees, Forests and Binary Trees
questions.explanation: A right-skewed chain occupies positions up to 2^(h+1) − 1 = 1023, wasting most of them.

sets.name: 2 · Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees

questions.question: In a threaded binary tree, the NULL child pointers are replaced by:

options.D: Pointers (threads) to the inorder predecessor and successor

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Threads allow inorder traversal without a stack or recursion.

questions.question: A binary tree with n nodes has how many threads when it is fully (doubly) threaded?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: They replace the n + 1 NULL pointers (some implementations point the extreme ones to a header node).

questions.question: In a right-threaded binary tree, the right thread of a node points to its:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Left threads point to inorder predecessors.

questions.question: The main advantage of a threaded binary tree is that:

options.A: It uses less memory for data
options.D: Inorder traversal can be done without recursion or a stack

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: A tag bit per pointer marks whether it is a child link or a thread.

questions.question: An inorder traversal of a binary search tree lists the keys in:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Left subtree < root < right subtree at every node.

questions.question: The keys 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, 80 are inserted in this order into an empty BST. What is the height of the tree?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: It forms a perfect tree: 50; 30 and 70; 20, 40, 60, 80.

questions.question: The keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 are inserted in this order into an empty BST. The tree's height is:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Sorted input makes a right-skewed chain.

questions.question: Searching for a key in a BST with n nodes takes, in the worst case:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: A skewed BST behaves like a linked list; a balanced one gives O(log n).

questions.question: The minimum key in a BST is found at:

options.D: The leftmost node, reached by following left pointers from the root

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: The maximum is at the rightmost node.

questions.question: To delete a BST node that has two children, it is usually replaced by its:

options.B: Inorder successor (the minimum of its right subtree) or inorder predecessor

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: That keeps the BST ordering intact.

questions.question: A BST has preorder 30 20 10 25 40 35 50. Its postorder traversal is:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Root 30; left subtree 20 (10, 25); right subtree 40 (35, 50).

questions.question: How many different BSTs can be built from the keys 1, 2, 3?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: The count is the Catalan number C₃ = 5.

questions.question: The inorder successor of a BST node that has a right subtree is:

options.D: The leftmost node of its right subtree

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: If there is no right subtree, it is the nearest ancestor of which the node lies in the left subtree.

questions.question: Keys 45, 15, 79, 90, 10, 55, 12, 20, 50 are inserted into an empty BST. How many comparisons (key tests) are needed to find 50?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: 50 is compared with 45 → 79 → 55 → 50.

questions.question: Deleting a leaf node from a BST requires:

options.A: Only setting its parent's pointer to NULL

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Leaves have no subtrees to reattach.

questions.question: Which sequence of keys, inserted in order, gives the most balanced BST for 1–7?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Inserting the median first at each level builds a perfect tree of height 2.

questions.question: The average-case time for search, insert and delete in a BST built from random keys is:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Random insertion orders give an expected height of O(log n).

questions.question:
Match the operation with where it looks in a BST:
a. Find minimum
b. Find maximum
c. Inorder successor of a node with a right subtree
d. Sorted listing

1. Rightmost node
2. Inorder traversal
3. Leftmost node of the right subtree
4. Leftmost node
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: All follow from the BST ordering property.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In a BST, every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key.
II. A BST never needs more than O(log n) time for a search.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: An unbalanced (skewed) BST needs O(n) time.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A threaded binary tree needs a flag with each pointer to tell a thread from a child link.
II. Threads make inorder traversal possible in O(n) time without extra stack space.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Both statements are correct.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Inserting keys into a BST in sorted order gives a skewed tree.
Reason (R): Each new key is larger than all earlier keys, so it always goes to the rightmost position.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: That produces a chain of right children.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Inorder traversal of a BST gives the keys in descending order.
Reason (R): In a BST, keys in the left subtree are smaller than the root.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Because left keys are smaller, inorder is ascending; A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Deleting a BST node with two children can be done by copying its inorder successor into it.
Reason (R): The inorder successor of such a node has at most one child.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Both true; the reason A works is that the successor keeps the ordering; R explains why deleting the successor afterwards is easy.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Threaded binary trees remove the need for a stack in inorder traversal.
Reason (R): Threaded binary trees are always height-balanced.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: A is true; R is false – threading says nothing about balance.

questions.question: The maximum number of comparisons needed to search a BST of height h is:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: One comparison per level along the longest path.

questions.question: Which of these binary search trees would give the WORST search time?

options.A: One built by inserting 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 in order

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Sorted insertion creates height 6 instead of 2.

questions.question: In a BST, the key 50 is searched for along the path 60 → 30 → 45 → 55 → 50. Which statement is correct?

options.D: It is a valid BST search path

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: 60 (go left), 30 (right), 45 (right), 55 (left), 50: every step is consistent with the key 50.

questions.question: The left child of a node x in a BST has the key 40 and the right child has the key 70. Which key can x have?
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: x must be greater than every key in its left subtree and smaller than every key in its right subtree.

questions.question: A BST is used to store a dictionary where many insertions arrive in sorted order. The best fix is to:

options.A: Store the keys in a stack
options.D: Use a self-balancing tree such as an AVL tree

questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: Self-balancing trees keep the height O(log n).

questions.question: In a threaded tree, the leftmost node's left thread and the rightmost node's right thread usually point to:
questions.subject: Threaded Binary Trees and Binary Search Trees
questions.explanation: The header node closes the thread chain.

questions.question: The balance factor of a node in an AVL tree is defined as:

options.A: Number of left children − number of right children
options.C: Number of nodes in the subtree
options.D: Height of the left subtree − height of the right subtree

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: It must be −1, 0 or +1 at every node.

questions.question: An AVL tree is named after:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: They introduced it in 1962; it was the first self-balancing BST.

questions.question: Inserting into the left subtree of a node's left child makes the node unbalanced (LL case). The fix is:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: The RR case is fixed by a single left rotation.

questions.question: The LR case (insertion into the right subtree of the left child) is fixed by:

options.D: A left rotation at the left child followed by a right rotation at the unbalanced node

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: The RL case is the mirror image: right rotation, then left rotation.

questions.question: 10, 20 and 30 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. The root of the final tree is:

options.C: The tree has no single root

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: RR imbalance at 10 is fixed by a left rotation, making 20 the root.

questions.question: 30, 10 and 20 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. Which rotation is needed?
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: 20 goes into the right subtree of 30's left child 10; the result has 20 at the root.

questions.question: The keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. The root of the final tree is:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: The rotations produce the perfect tree 4 (2 (1, 3), 6 (5, 7)).

questions.question: The height of the AVL tree formed by inserting 1 to 7 in order is:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Compare this with a plain BST, whose height would be 6.

questions.question: The minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 3 is:
questions.subject: AVL Trees

questions.question: The minimum number of nodes in an AVL tree of height 4 is:
questions.subject: AVL Trees

questions.question: Search, insertion and deletion in an AVL tree of n nodes take:

options.A: O(log n) time in the worst case
options.D: O(n) time in the worst case

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Its height is always O(log n) (at most about 1.44 log₂ n).

questions.question: After an insertion into an AVL tree, how many rotations (single or double) are needed at most to restore balance?
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Fixing the lowest unbalanced ancestor restores its original height; deletions may need O(log n) rotations.

questions.question: A node has a left subtree of height 3 and a right subtree of height 1. Its balance factor and status are:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: 3 − 1 = 2, which is outside −1..+1.

questions.question: Compared with a red–black tree, an AVL tree is:

options.A: Less balanced than a red–black tree
options.C: More strictly balanced, giving faster lookups but possibly more rotations on updates

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Red–black trees allow heights up to 2 log₂(n + 1).

questions.question: A single left rotation at node x (with right child y) makes:

options.A: x the right child of y
options.B: y the new root of the subtree, x its left child, and y's old left subtree x's right subtree
options.C: y the left child of x
options.D: No change in the inorder sequence and no change in shape

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Rotations preserve the inorder (BST) order.

questions.question:
Match the imbalance case with its fix:
a. LL
b. RR
c. LR
d. RL

1. Left rotation of the left child, then right rotation
2. Right rotation of the right child, then left rotation
3. Single right rotation
4. Single left rotation
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: The case names describe the path from the unbalanced node to the new node.

questions.question: 50, 40 and 30 are inserted in this order into an empty AVL tree. After rebalancing, the preorder traversal is:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: An LL imbalance at 50 is fixed by a right rotation, making 40 the root.

questions.question: An AVL tree has 20 nodes. Its height can be at most:
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: The minimum node counts are N(4) = 12 and N(5) = 20, so 20 nodes can reach height 5 but not 6 (N(6) = 33).

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Every AVL tree is a binary search tree.
II. Every binary search tree is an AVL tree.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Only BSTs whose nodes all have balance factors −1, 0 or +1 are AVL trees.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Rotations in an AVL tree preserve the inorder sequence of keys.
II. After an insertion, only nodes on the path from the new node to the root can become unbalanced.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: Only heights along the insertion path change, and rotations keep the BST order.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Searching an AVL tree takes O(log n) time even in the worst case.
Reason (R): An AVL tree's height is always O(log n).

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: AVL Trees
questions.explanation: The search cost is bounded by the height.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Inserting keys in sorted order makes an AVL tree skewed.
Reason (R): AVL trees rebalance themselves using rotations after insertions.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
